gaps: While several papers discuss multi-agent systems and LLM-based software engineering, there is no research that integrates event sourcing with security auditing in autonomous agent workflows. The absence of event-driven, auditable trails for agent actions—especially in security-sensitive contexts—leaves systems vulnerable to unauthorized or unintended behavior. Papers such as [2025] Cybersecurity Threat Intelligence for Audit and [2025] SECURITY AS CODE USING AGENTIC AI highlight security concern

Although [2025] Information Security, Ethics, and Integrity in LLM Agent Interaction acknowledges ethical concerns, it does not provide a framework for embedding real-time ethical decision-making into agent workflows. There is no research on how agents can dynamically evaluate ethical implications of their actions during execution, nor how such evaluations are audited or enforced.

Despite growing interest in multi-agent LLM frameworks, there is no work that formally verifies the correctness or safety of decision chains generated by LLM-powered agents. This includes validation of logical consistency, adherence to constraints, and resistance to adversarial inputs. Papers like [2025] ALMAS and [2025] Di-Agent describe agent architectures but do not address formal methods for validating agent behavior or ensuring correctness in critical systems.

The paper [2026] The Evolution of Tool Use in LLM Agents: From Single-Tool Call to Multi-Tool Orchestration describes tool use evolution but does not explore how such tool orchestration interacts with event sourcing architectures. There is no research on how agent tool calls are eventized, how state transitions are captured, and how these events support consistency and recovery in distributed agent systems.

While papers such as [2025] Identifying Performance-Sensitive Configurations and [2025] Using CQRS and Event Sourcing in the Architecture of Complex Software Solutions describe technical frameworks, there is a lack of empirical evaluation of how these agents perform in actual software development environments. No paper provides measurable outcomes on code quality, developer productivity, or bug rates under real-world conditions.
